That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

part.title: Welcome to the university library

turns.text: Hi everyone, and welcome to Hartwell Library. My name's Dana Whitmore, and I'm one of the librarians here. Over the next twenty minutes or so, I'll tell you how borrowing works, where you can study, and what kind of help you can get. So, let's start with borrowing.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Your student card is also your library card, so there's nothing extra to sign up for. Now, a lot of you will have heard that undergraduates can take out ten items at a time. That was true until last year, but the limit's now fifteen. Graduate students can have twenty, but for you, it's fifteen.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Okay, what if you keep something too long? We actually got rid of daily fines a couple of years ago, so you won't be paying a few cents a day. What happens instead is that your account gets frozen, so you can't check out anything else until the late item comes back. We'll only send you a bill for the replacement cost if something's more than six weeks overdue.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Right, course reserves. These are books your professors have put aside because the whole class needs them, and they're kept behind the main service desk. Some of you might think you can only read them inside the building. That used to be the rule, but these days you can take them out for up to four hours at a time. And you don't need to request them online or anything; just ask at the desk.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Let's move on to online resources. We subscribe to thousands of journals and e-books, and you can get to all of them from home. A few years ago, you had to install special software on your laptop to do that. Now you just sign in through the library website with the same email and password you use for everything else on campus. There's no need to register with us separately.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: And if we don't have something, we can borrow it from another library for you. That's called an interlibrary loan, and it's free. Journal articles are quickest; they usually arrive by email in two or three days. Books take a bit longer, normally about a week, although something rare or very old can take up to a month.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: We also run workshops all semester, on things like citing sources and searching databases. Some new students also rush to book one-on-one appointments with a librarian in their first week. But honestly, the first thing I'd ask you to do is the online orientation tutorial on our website. It only takes about twenty minutes, and it'll answer most of your questions before you even have them.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Okay, now let me tell you about some of the spaces and services you'll see as we walk around. First, the group study rooms on the third floor. You can reserve them on our website up to seven days in advance, and I'd recommend that, because they fill up fast. And there's a myth that they're only for final-year students. That's not true at all; anyone can book them.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Next, the silent reading room on the fourth floor. It's completely quiet, and to keep it that way, you're not allowed to bring bags inside. There are lockers just outside the door for that. Some people ask if it stays open all night during exams. It doesn't, I'm afraid; that's the twenty-four-hour lounge on the ground floor.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: If your own laptop breaks down, don't panic. You can borrow one of ours from the service desk, using your student card. They're very popular, so the rule is they have to come back to the desk before we close that same evening. You can't keep them overnight.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Then there's the writing center, where tutors help you plan and improve your essays. If you've seen old maps of the building, they show it on the second floor. But over the summer it moved down to the basement, next to the computer lab, so that's where you'll find it now.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Printing. Printers are on every floor, and you pay with your student card. Each semester, the first hundred pages are free, so you don't pay anything until you've used those up. After that it's ten cents a page, sorry, eight cents, for black and white.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: And finally, the subject librarians. Every department has one, and they're the people to talk to about research for your assignments. During the day you can drop by their offices on the first floor, but a lot of students have classes then, so they also offer video calls in the evenings, until about nine. You'll find the links on the library website.
turns.speaker: librarian

turns.text: Okay, that's the overview. Let's head upstairs, and I'll show you the third floor first.
turns.speaker: librarian

Then there's the writing center, where tutors help you plan and improve your essays. If you've seen old maps of the building, they show it on the second floor, but over the summer it moved down to the basement, next to the computer lab, so that's where you'll find it now.

Printing. Printers are on every floor, and you pay with your student card. Each semester, the first hundred pages are free, so you don't pay anything until you've used those up. After that it's ten cents a page, sorry, eight cents, for black and white.

And finally, the subject librarians. Every department has one, and they're the people to talk to about research for your assignments. During the day you can drop by their offices on the first floor, but a lot of students have classes then, so they also offer video calls in the evenings, until about nine.
